landscape: Legislative data have long centred on the United States Congress. Voteview's roll-call record runs from 1789 to the present, and around it sit the Congressional Bills Project, the Legislative Effectiveness Scores, Stewart's committee data and a dense set of official sources (Congress.gov, GovInfo, Bioguide). The American states have comparable resources: Shor-McCarty ideal points, Open States and LegiScan bill data, and the Squire professionalism index.

Comparative legislative data have grown fast in the last decade. The Comparative Legislators Database, the Global Legislators Database and LALD describe who legislators are. ParlSpeech and several parliamentary-question datasets capture what they say. Roll-call datasets now exist for the European Parliament and for a growing number of national parliaments, including Germany, the Netherlands and Portugal. Many parliaments also publish open data through official APIs, which this chapter lists as portals.

Data fragility is a recurring theme. Of the 87 LEG rows, 26 are frozen and 4 discontinued. Several well-used resources have disappeared or changed hands: the Congressional Bills Project's own domain now redirects to an unrelated commercial site, VoteWatch Europe closed and survives only as an archive, and the Parltrack and EUPLEX hosts are unreachable. Wherever a persistent repository copy exists, prefer it over a project website.

core.text: Voteview provides every recorded vote in the U.S. House and Senate since 1789, together with DW-NOMINATE ideal points for every member. It is updated continuously and has no numbered versions. It is widely used to study congressional ideology and polarisation. The first dimension summarises voting patterns that agenda control and party pressure also shape, so it is not a pure measure of personal ideology (Lee 2009). Pin a download date for replication.

The Legislative Effectiveness Scores measure how far each legislator moves their sponsored bills through the lawmaking process, weighted by bill significance. They cover members of Congress from 1973 and members of state legislatures, and they are widely used to measure individual legislative productivity. They miss influence exercised through amendments and negotiation, and a method change from the 117th Congress creates a break in the series.

The Comparative Legislators Database links biographical, career and social-media data for about 68,000 politicians in 16 countries to Wikipedia and Wikidata identifiers, and it is accessible through the legislatoR package. It is a practical starting point for comparative legislator studies. Its completeness, however, inherits Wikipedia's uneven coverage, and it has not been updated since 2023.

IPU Parline is a database on the world's national parliaments: chamber structure, electoral system, membership size, women's and young members' representation, and election results, with an open API. Its data are reported by the parliaments themselves. For many fields current values overwrite earlier ones, so extractions should be dated and archived.

ParlSpeech offers full-text plenary speeches with speaker, party and date for the lower chambers of nine democracies, mostly from the late 1980s to 2016-2019. It is often used for comparative text-as-data studies of parliamentary debate. Version 2 is frozen. Its successor project, ParlLawSpeech, links speeches to legislation but does not cover all of the same parliaments.

choosing: Roll-call measures summarise recorded votes, which are a selected subset of legislative decisions in most parliaments outside the U.S. Congress. This selection problem is documented for the European Parliament by Carrubba et al. (2006) and Hug (2010). Where recorded votes are rare or strategically requested, prefer speech-, question- or bill-based measures, or model the selection explicitly.

Biographical datasets built from Wikipedia are broad but uneven. Official sources such as Bioguide, Parline and national portals are authoritative but harder to compare across countries. Link through persistent identifiers (Wikidata, ICPSR codes, Bioguide IDs) rather than names.
gaps: Roll-call and bill data for parliaments outside Europe and the Americas are rare; Africa is represented only by a 13-country legislative agenda dataset and the Kenyan Mzalendo exports.
No maintained cross-national dataset of legislative powers exists since the Parliamentary Powers Index, whose scores survive only in print.

Several European Parliament resources (Hix-Noury-Roland roll calls, VoteWatch, Parltrack, the Oslo database) have ended or become unreachable; HowTheyVote.eu and the official EP open-data portal now carry most current coverage.
